utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And finally, 03742. That's from 2006, the Main Staff Command Responsibility Report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Correct, sir. In this particular case or the next particular case in chronological order that I was involved in was the Popovic case. utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.text: Very well. How many of them? Six of them? They will be all admitted. Shall we give them numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And we will need to upload just that section H. It's not separated out yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to do now, Mr. Butler, is go through just a little bit of background before we get to July 1995 and explain a little bit of the context of what we see happening from March through August 1995 in the Srebrenica area. You were not able to do a specific report for this case, but there is some information, quite a lot of information in your other reports about the role of the Supreme Commander. In your VRS Main Staff Command Responsibility Report, page 9, paragraph 2.1, you wrote the following: "In accordance with the relevant laws of the Republika Srpska at the time, the pinnacle of command of the RS armed forces was the president of the republic functioning as a commander-in-chief of the armed forces." And there you cited to Article 174 and other relevant portions of the Law on the Army. I'd just like to ask you to expand on that a little bit as president and Supreme Commander, what forces would Radovan Karadzic have had under his command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the context of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska there were two primary bodies that fell under that umbrella. The first one was the army, and incorporated, of course, in the army were the air and air defence forces; and the second component of the armed forces was the forces of the Ministry of the Interior which would include primarily in the context of battle-field operations the various police and special police units that were raised and organised and maintained during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And over the next -- today and the next couple of days we'll discuss the command function over those forces as well as reporting down the command chain. What I want to ask you about now is the creation of the Drina Corps in 1992. You talk about that in your revised narrative, chapter 1, page 6, paragraph 1, right at the beginning of the narrative, and maybe it would help if we looked at the map book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 65 ter number 23519, map A3. That's page 5 in e-court but it's easier to see, I think, in the hard copy but we can bring it up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, can you just tell us if that's an accurate representation of the boundaries in general of the Drina Corps and why this corps was created as, I believe, the last of six corps of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This map is generally accurate to my knowledge. It reflects the geographical boundaries that existed after November 1992 with the creation of the Drina Corps. Unlike the other five corps of the Army of Republika Srpska that were organised at the very earliest part of the war in April and May of 1992, the Drina Corps was not established until November of 1992, in part because the other five remaining corps of the VRS have what I refer to as a lineage back to the JNA. They were based on the organisation and structure of existing JNA corps at the time that the war began in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Drina Corps did not. There were no significant JNA units of any size in Eastern Bosnia south of Bijeljina at the beginning of the war, so that area was divided between the East Bosnia Corps and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. As time and history would note, the forces that the VRS and the attention that the VRS command paid to Eastern Bosnia was inadequate to deal with the military threat posed by the considerable amount of Bosnian Muslim military units that were operating in the area. And in late October, as manifested in early November of 1992, the army determined that the military situation could be best addressed by re-organising the area designating a sixth VRS corps command headquarters, in this case the Drina Corps in Vlasenica, and reassigning various combat units that previously belonged to East Bosnia Corps and Sarajevo-Romanija Corps under the command of the Drina Corps. So that particular geographical area now had its own corps-level command to plan and execute larger operations and subordinate brigades to it to undertake those operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could briefly tell us you -- you spoke there about the -- the threat or the -- from the Muslim forces. Could you just tell us briefly, what was the situation facing the VRS or the Bosnian Serb armed forces and the Bosnian Serb population in that area around November 1st, 1992, when the Drina Corps was created.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, first off, particularly in the municipalities -- the key municipalities bordering the Drina River, the Zvornik municipality, the Bratunac municipality, the Vlasenica-Milici municipality, and even further south towards Zepa, Visegrad, Rogatica, Bosnian Muslims were the dominant population group. So even though Bosnian Serb territorial forces and locally raised militia units were successful in capturing and holding the town population centres such as Zvornik, Bratunac, Vlasenica, and even for a little while Srebrenica before it was recaptured, there were wide areas of the countryside that were not under control of the Bosnian Serb armed forces. In the early parts of 1992 when the most critical terrain for the establishment and survival of what would then become the Republika Srpska was the Posavina Corridor, that corridor between the Krajina and Eastern Bosnia, the Bosnian Serbs had no choice but to accept risk and basically the Eastern Bosnia area was not the highest priority of the conflict. Once the Posavina Corridor area was secured and the Republika Srpska could count on continued territorial integrity between Eastern Bosnia and the Krajina, that began the shift to the next critical area for the establishment and -- or maintenance of the Republika Srpska which is dealing with the military situation in Eastern Bosnia, where they recognised by November 1992 was particularly dire from their point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for our information, could you ask the witness to mark the Posavina Corridor on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Butler, could you just mark the area you were talking about, the corridor which was the first major military operation that needed to be achieved by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would be on this boundary region between the East Bosnia Corps and the 1st Krajina Corps area. So both those corps were particularly engaged in those combat activities for a number of months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could date and your initial -- put your initials.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And once that's saved, could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, what's going to come up in front of you is a map have depicting the Drina Corps area of responsibility. So more detail on the area than we see on the present map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's just speak now of summer of 1995. Can you tell me if these boundaries are reasonably accurate regarding the different brigades within the Drina Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we admitted this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We haven't, Your Honour, and what I was going to attempt to do later on at the conclusion of Mr. Butler's testimony - I won't go through every map but several of these - is admit the map book as a whole, because we've been using it throughout the trial so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I'd like to do now, Mr. Butler, is again briefly go through some charts which were originally appended to your narrative. These are slightly -- they are updated of the Main Staff, Drina Corps, and then of the Zvornik and Bratunac brigades, the two key brigades for our topics today, and I'll -- with the assistant of the usher if I could pass you a copy of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is -- 23702 is the number we've assigned to this packet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I won't spend a lot of time on the Main Staff chart, Mr. Butler, because we've had some evidence on it and some testimony, but looking at this, could you just look at it quickly, look at the structure we have here and the assistant commanders for the different sectors --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you give the 65 ter number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 23702, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So as of July 1995, based on all the research you did into the Srebrenica events, is this a good depiction of the different officers in charge of the different sectors and their subordinates and the structure of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. General Krstic, Major-General Krstic, was his Chief of Staff. On the evening of 13 July 1995, General Zivanovic was ultimately reassigned and retired, and General Krstic then assumed the position of Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. So within the context that the chart is labelled July 1995, there were two corps commanders during that month because in the middle of the month there was a command change.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. In the answer, you've just said that on 13 July in the evening General Zivanovic was ultimately reassigned and retired, and General Krstic then assumed the position of Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, he was the Chief of Staff. He assumed the position as commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think that's clear if we go to the next chart of the Drina Corps. And sorry, one question - we don't need to go back to the map of the Main Staff - before we go on. Do you recall the code-name and communications used for the Main Staff in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In communications it was referred to as Panorama.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And now we have the Drina Corps chart. Same question. If you could look at this and tell us if this looks accurate to you, and we see here the notation of Krstic becoming commander on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the code-name for the Drina Corps in communications?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The common code-name for the Drina Corps in the communications was Zlatar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Next I just want to show the Zvornik Brigade chart. If we could have that. Again, July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you would just take a look at this for a minute and it's the same question. Does this accurately depict the structure for the period we're going to spend most of the time on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally -- oh, I'm sorry. What was the code-name for referring to Zvornik Brigade in communications?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER

utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted.

utterances.text: As Exhibit P4920, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I should say, Mr. Butler, you've got some binders with you that you brought into the courtroom. Is that a binder of your reports and then a binder of documents which were notified to be potentially used with your testimony that I provided you when you arrived here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to talk now a little bit continuing in November 1992. We talked about the creation of the corps in early November, and I want to talk about directive 4 now for just a minute. This is a topic you deal with in your revised narrative, beginning at page 12, paragraphs 1.22, 1.23, and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is P00976. If I could have that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I won't spend a lot of time on this, Mr. Butler because it's been discussed quite heavily in this trial, but I would like you view on it. Specifically if we look at English page 5. I think it's page 10 of the B/C/S. Tasks for the Drina Corps. While it's coming up, could you briefly tell us based on your expertise, your study, how would you define a Main Staff directive such as this directive? What are they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: While these particular directives are drafted by the Main Staff, what they represented was the highest level of political-military direction for the conduct of the war. I believe during the course of the conflict there were a total of nine strategic directives that were published, and at various points in time in the conflict, there were occasions where the goals, and again the strategic goals, of the Republika Srpska changed or were established or new ones were established which were occasions where the Main Staff would draft a document for ultimately the approval of the Supreme Command, which would reflect their strategic understanding of the conflict as it was ongoing, their understanding of what the political strategic goals of the leadership of the Republika Srpska were, and their proposals in that sense as to how the military forces of the Army of the Republika Srpska would be organised and the operations that they would undertake in order to best achieve those solutions. And again in this context, the military drafted the document and the language after negotiation with the various other entities that were involved, primarily the Supreme Command in the Ministry of the Interior. They would send it up to the Supreme Command for ratification, and you see that more in the later versions than the earlier versions. The Supreme Command wasn't formed until late in 1992, early 1993 period operational. So those documents at the highest level represent the military's view of how they're going to undertake the strategic conduct of the conflict that they were engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I should have said this is at tab 1 of your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I should have said this is at tab 1 of your binder. If we look at paragraph marked (D) which assigns task to the Drina Corps: "From its present position, its main forces are to defend with utmost persistence Visegrad (the dam), Zvornik and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region are to exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on them, and force them with the Muslim population to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas." And this directive we've seen before was drafted by General Manojlo Milovanovic. My question is: If you could comment on that portion of the directive and whether and how it relates to subsequent military operations we see in the Podrinje area.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As discussed, even in November of 1992, December 1992, January/February of 1993, there were far more Bosnian Muslims residing in Eastern Bosnia and particularly in the Drina Corps zone than there were Bosnian Serbs, although the Bosnian Serb military held the towns and the key communications routes, the roads, between them. This particular operation again was not only to destroy the various military forces but to create the conditions so that the underlying Bosnian Muslim civilian population would leave those particular regions, and in fact, if you go through the various months, January, February, March of 1993, and watch how the operations are conducted and the ultimate results, it's clear that the Bosnian Muslim civilian populations in those areas, particularly, for example, the Cerska area, took one of two courses of action. They either fled or were pushed to the west and ultimately towards Tuzla, or they were -- they fled or were pushed towards the south and clustered in and around the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could have P03037.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 2, Mr. Butler, of your binder. This is from the Main Staff to the command of the Drina Corps, the approximately three-week old Drina Corps. And it states: "Pursuant to the request by the Supreme Command of the Army of Republika Srpska (President of the Presidency Dr. Radovan Karadzic), and with a view to carrying out timely preparation and holding a military and political seminar at the level of the Drina Corps, I hereby order," and then it continues to describe the seminar that will take place on 23rd November which will be chaired and attended by President Karadzic. Can you just comment on that document and what it tell us about the Supreme Commander and the political leadership's connection to this newly formed corps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, sir, at its face, I mean, it notes that the president of the Presidency at this time, Dr. Karadzic, requests the Supreme -- he's the Supreme Command -- in this case the Supreme Commander of the Army of Republika Srpska, it notes that that there's going to be a meeting specific at his request with respect to the newly organised Drina Corps, and not only do they want the military commanders of the various units of the Drina Corps at this particular meeting, they want the various municipal authority presidents to attend this meeting as well. And within the context of what was happening in the Drina Corps area at that time, there was a lot of infighting and miscommunication between the military and the civilian leadership of the various municipalities over the goals and the objectives and ultimately even the control of some military units. So given the fact that this new corps headquarters is standing itself up, it's organising its missions, it's organising its forces, and from the timing it sounds like, you know, in context an excellent opportunity for the highest political and military leadership to be on the ground at the Drina Corps headquarters where they can fully synchronise the military and political objectives of what's going to be happening in Eastern Bosnia in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this -- and this urgent order on the 20th of November, that's the day after directive 4 that we just looked at; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I now have P04248, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 4, Mr. Butler. It's the timetable for the conference to be held on the 23rd of November and it lists the speakers, beginning with Dr. Karadzic. And we see commander of the Drina Corps Colonel Zivanovic will speak second, and then the various brigade commanders, Krstic, Kusic, Pandurevic, on the next page Andric, and then it's closed by Dr. President Karadzic. Could you just comment on this document and also on who some of the people I named are, whether they are still around performing roles in July 1995 in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, most in this context it lays out the time allotted for each brigade -- for each brigade commander to update the situation in his brigade area as well as the capabilities of his units and to essentially brief back to the key military and civilian leadership what he understands his task to be. Again, not necessarily the interesting but the unique thing about this is that many of the individuals who are named here in November of 1992 are still key figures within the context of the Drina Corps in July of 1995 respecting -- you know, reflecting a long three-year historical association with all of the activities in Eastern Bosnia. For example, at the beginning of July 1995, then General Zivanovic is still the corps commander. So he's fully familiar with the history of Eastern Bosnia from November of 1992 all the way until the last day of his command, 13 July. Then Colonel Krstic is a brigade commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade in July -- in -- in 1995, I think it's in March, he becomes the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, and of course on 13 July 1995, he assumes command of the Drina Corps. So he has a long historical association with the history of Eastern Bosnia. Captain Kusic remains with his unit throughout the course of the entire war. Colonel Pandurevic at this time is the commander of the 5th Podrinje Unit -- or Brigade, otherwise known as the Visegrad Brigade in this context. He -- well, I'm sorry, the Gorazde Brigade in this context. He, in December of 1992, was appointed to be the commander of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, and he remains the commander of that brigade through the end of the war in November of 1995. So again he has a long historical association with what is happening in the Eastern Bosnia area. The same can be said of, the second page, Colonel Andric, who begins the war as the commander of the Birac Brigade. At this time they're still separating the Zvornik and Birac brigades out a bit. But -- or in this context the Birac Brigade. He then turns around and, you know, remains the commander through 13 July, and on 13 July of 1995, he's elevated to take the role as the corps Chief of Staff. So I mean this just reflects in the military context many of the key individuals who participate in Srebrenica in July 1995 have a long historical association with the VRS military operations in Eastern Bosnia from almost the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 10881.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is back at tab 3, Mr. Butler. This is an urgent order from Milenko Zivanovic, the corps commander, which states that this conference we've been talking about will be led personally by the Supreme Commander of the Republika Srpska Army. Could you -- we've talked about this a bit, but could you just comment on that portion of the document, what it tells us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, again in this particular document, and I'm sure that people have discussed prior to me, General Mladic was the commander of the Main Staff. He was the senior uniformed army member, but it is recognised ultimately that the president of the republic under the law of the Republika Srpska is the Supreme Commander of the army and armed forces in this particular context. It is their acknowledgement of such that the president of the republic is going to be at this meeting and it is expected that, you know, all of the key military principals, and that will be the brigade commanders personally, will be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both of them, with the timetable as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the timetable is already admitted as P04248.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4921, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter 10728.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 5 in your binder, Mr. Butler. This is dated 23 November 1992. It's a daily combat report. The part I'm interested in most is paragraph 2 towards the end. It speaks about providing security for the RS Assembly and then states: "During the day, a military-political conference was held at the garrison command attended by the representatives of the Supreme Command, the Army of Republika Srpska, as well as members of the political structures." It's pretty self-apparent, but does this show that this conference actually took place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P4922, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Next could I have P02716.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 6, Mr. Butler. E-court page 40 in English, I believe 41 in the original. And, Mr. Butler, this is Mr. Karadzic's notebook from the time. I'm looking at the heading, the entry for 23rd November 1992, the day of the conference, and we've got written: Consultations, Drina Corps commander, chief of GS [sic] Main Staff, Minister of Defence Colonel Subotic, and General Gvero, brigade commanders, and municipal presidents. And then we see Colonel Zivanovic, who we can remember was the first speaker after President Karadzic at the conference, and the notes read: "Tasks. Vitinica, Sapna, Teocak," under 1; 2, Cerska; 3, Zepa; 4, Srebrenica; and 5, Gorazde. Now can you tell us what is the military significance of those areas spoken about by the corps commander General Zivanovic at this time, November 1992, a couple days after directive 4's come out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: During that time-frame those were all areas that were either already under the control of Bosnian Muslim military forces or significantly threatened by them, and this appears to be a ranking in priority of order of what the corps commander believes his priority areas are to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's -- excuse me. That's that topic finished. I now want to move on to directive 7, moving into 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have that up, please. It's P00838.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll go through this pretty quickly, because Their Honours have seen this quite a few times, Mr. Butler. It's tab 7 of your binder. If we could get the English page 10 and the Serbian page 14. Now, this is -- this is the section on the Drina Corps you're very familiar with, I know, Mr. Butler. But the section which speaks of: "... as many enemy forces as possible should be tied down by diversionary and active combat operations on the north-west part of the front using operational and tactical camouflage measures, while in the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves. By planned and well-thought out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." And then on page 14 of the English, which I believe is 21 of the Serbian, under the section of the directive headed "Support for combat operations. Morale and psychological support," we see: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits reduce and limit the logistic support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community." And I won't go through the other sections, just for time, of this directive, but the question is: Can you comment on this directive and militarily any connection you see with what we saw in directive 4 in the goals that were announced in November 1992 now that we're in March 1995.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Notwithstanding the creation of the -- the UN safe areas of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, the VRS's goal as reflected in the military documents in that context has always been clear, and again even as they note in the last line of the top paragraph of page 11 of directive 7, they're still talking about the definitive liberation of the Drina valley region. In their mind, particularly with the history of what happened in late 1992 and in early 1993 in areas such as Bratunac, I don't believe that there was any thought that there could possibly be some form of an accommodation to live with a sizable Muslim population in those areas. There was just too much bad history as a result of what had happened. The Bosnian Serb military forces had always -- in various other documents as well had made it clear that, one, they wanted the safe areas eliminated completely for military reasons and that their history, particularly with the Srebrenica and Zepa safe areas, was that allowing the Muslim population to remain there in effect meant that there would be Muslim military units there, which would be unacceptable. So I mean, I think their goals from directive 4 to directive 7 in that context never changed. It was just they had to accept a United Nations presence for three years in Eastern Bosnia and seek somehow to get around that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So what you just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to continue on that, what from your analysis and then looking at what happened afterwards, which we'll discuss, was the objective of directive 7?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, directive 7 as noted here didn't call for a direct military assault on the enclaves, and clearly with what was going on at the international level, that was deemed to be too provocative. But what they were looking to do was create a situation where either the UN themselves would quit these areas or that the Bosnian Muslim population residing in them would pressure their own leadership in Sarajevo to withdraw them. I think I've said in previous testimony, ultimately they wanted to recreate the situation that existed in the spring of 1993 where the population of the Srebrenica safe area specifically was in such dire straits that the United Nations was actively evacuating the population to other -- other areas of Bosnian Muslim-held territory, and that ultimately was what they would have liked to see again as a way of finally handling the issue of the safe areas by the end of July -- or by the end of 1995 or through the end of the operative period of directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I now have P02246.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this is at tab 8 of your binder, and it's directive 7/1. Directive 7/1 is from 31st of March, 1995. There's been some discussion about it in this trial. It's much shorter than directive 7. It doesn't contain all the language of directive 7 including the parts I read out. Can you tell us what's the purpose? What does this operative directive number 7/1 do, and does it supplant, replace, or negate directive 7? Sorry, that's a compound question, but I think you can put it together.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: To answer the last question first, no, it does not negate or otherwise supplant directive 7. What directive 7/1 represents is a technical expansion of the goals of directive 7 more designed for military planners. For example, when you look at this particular document, it gives more concrete definable goals that can be carried out by military organisations naming various towns, cities, and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you for one second. Maybe we could go to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe we can go to page 5 then and look at paragraph 5.3 of the English. Also page 5 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, that is an excellent example. When you look at directive 7.0, you have a broad task which is, you know, to create an unbearable situation against the civilian population. For a military planner, the first question is, well, what does that mean? What am I supposed to do? As you notice now in directive 7/1 geared more toward military individuals, they're talking in more concrete terms. There are going to be various operations down various axes of attacks and these are the things that we're going to seek to accomplish. So again it's not replacing 7.0 in any way. This is just a more technical explanation of what the goals of 7.0 are. So that is my interpretation of what 7-1 is or 7.1 is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And under the way the VRS worked at the time based on your study, you've talked about the level of directives at the -- at this sort of highest level of goals, do the corps have a role in planning operations themselves that are to take place in their area which are based on directives or higher orders from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Particularly within the VRS, which for the most part wholly adopted the doctrine of the former Yugoslav National Army which was a well-developed military doctrine, their officers had been intensively and significantly trained in it, there was a formalised planning process which various military units undertook. While the Main Staff is -- is obviously the pinnacle of the military leadership with respect to the uniformed military in Bosnia, the reality is that the corps commands and the corps commanders were the people who ultimately were fighting the war on behalf of the Main Staff. These were the people who best understood the capabilities and the limitations of their military units as well as the terrain that they were be expected to fight on. So the practice was that while the Main Staff would give general guidance on various objectives and things of that nature, it was the responsibility of the corps to plan the details of the operation, and then once the planning of the operation was put together to the satisfaction of the corps commander, the corps command itself would then brief the details of that operation to their superior, which was the Main Staff. The Main Staff would review that operation and ultimately either seek -- approve the operation, they would disapprove it or they would make whatever changes they deemed were required. Not only did this process happen from the corps level to the Main Staff, but subordinate units as well. Brigade commanders planned military operations for their brigades, and those operations were reviewed and endorsed or approved by the superior corps commander. So that is the way that the former JNA military command and staff process worked, and it was adopted and followed as such by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll talk about that a bit more when we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Nicholls. Going back to the directive 7/1, were there any other instances than the case of directive 7/1 where either the command of the -- either the Supreme Commander or the Main Staff issued a further directive which you referred to as a technical expansion, other than the case of 7/1. After issuing a specific directive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure of the answer prior to that. I think in the case of directive 9 there might have been a supplemental if I recall correctly, but I just don't remember at this point in time if in some of the previous directives or in the previous ones, such as 6 or before that, they had a need to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll come back to that topic raised by His Honour the Presiding Judge in a little while, Mr. Butler, and ask you a couple questions, but first to keep moving, I'd like to ask you now a bit about the use of the MUP forces in military operations. In your brigade report you discuss this, for instance, at pages 30 to 31, paragraph 6.0. You talked about it a little bit at the beginning today. In that paragraph you wrote: "Aside from the forces of the army, VRS, the other component of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska consists of the units and forces of the Ministry of the Interior MUP police. These MUP assets when used under the purview of national defence are directed by the president of the republic under both the RS constitution and the RS Law on Defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And with that I'd like to bring up 65 ter number 1882, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's tab 9 in your binder, Mr. Butler. This document is from the Supreme Commander, Dr. Karadzic, has the seals and stamps of the Republika Srpska president. It's from the 22nd of April, 1995, and concerns the use of the MUP in combat. And I won't go through it all, but could you tell us about this document, what it means? And I'll just say as well that this is footnoted at footnotes 136, 138, and 139 of your brigade command report. That's kind of a broad question, but if you could give us your -- your comment on this document and what it tell us about use of the MUP in combat.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The MUP had historically been used to fight in combat operations with the VRS throughout the course of the conflict. They -- they represented a significant and potent fighting force. But historically within the framework of that there had always been issues related to the control of the MUP, co-ordination with those MUP forces, logistical responsibilities, who would support them, who would feed the soldiers, things of that nature. There were historical problems with soldiers often trying to defect to MUP units, and as part of regulating these things in a much more clearer manner, particularly in a state of imminent threat of war or a state of war, a number of laws were passed or revised relating to this. This particular document actually talks about specific articles of the law of the -- or the application of the Law on Interior -- on Internal Affairs during the state of an imminent threat of war and state of war, and it specifically talks about or clarifies issues relating to MUP forces falling under the command of the army and what those types of things meant. Now, keeping in mind that by decree, an imminent threat or an imminent threat of a state of war existed in the zones of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps since November of 1994, and again in June of 1995 that state of an imminent threat of war was declared for the entire Republika Srpska. So even though this document is dated in April, it's laying out the legal framework by which MUP forces will operate under army control and the limits to those controls that we would later see in June and July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we look at Articles 13 and 14 of the law, which are -- Dr. Karadzic has set out in this order of his. Police units shall participate in combat operations by order of the Supreme Commander of the armed forces and Ministry of the Interior. The minister of the interior commands police units via the staff of the command. And Article 14, having been engaged in combat activities by order of the Supreme Commander, and it continues. So what -- what's the role of the Supreme Commander in the designation of the use of the MUP in combat and the way they were used in combat?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, for the first part, ultimately it is the Supreme Commander who makes that decision, and it was a formalised process. The army would make a proposal to use MUP forces, and they would identify which forces they believed they need to -- through the military chain of command to the Supreme Command, and a decision would be made by the Supreme Command whether to accept that proposal, change it, modify it, or reject it. Now, in this particular context it's noted that the Ministry of the Interior is a member of the actual Supreme Command body that consisted of about five members who were actually designated as part of the Supreme Command. The military was represented there with respect to their proposals and ideas, but they were not formally part of the Supreme Command. So minister in this case -- you know, the minister of the interior was part of the decision to use his forces with the army. Once that decision was made, an order was sent down, and that particular order defined not what a particular MUP unit would do in a technical manner, the attack or things of that nature, but it would define the fact that this MUP unit was under military control for the duration -- I'm sorry -- for the duration of a particular operation, how long that would be, and set limits such as this unit could not be used for other purposes, it could not be disbanded, things of that nature. So again, those decisions were made by the Supreme Command and were transmitted down to the army and to the MUP for implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just -- thank you. And just we can see that this one is actually signed by the Supreme Commander, Dr. Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I intervene? I believe it's better to do it now than to burden the cross-examination with this. I'm afraid that the translation of the document is not right. And further on, it doesn't say that the minister commands. The minister is in charge of, and there is a difference. The last line of number 13. I cannot scroll down. Perhaps the interpreters could help. If they could read this out, but not line 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I thank Mr. Karadzic, but that's something we could check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that is noted. But would you like the accused to read out that sentence now or -- I'll leave it to you, Mr. Nicholls. In any event, your intervention has been noted and that will take care of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4923, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you agree, the more efficient way is to resolve it right now. Mr. Karadzic, why don't you read that, the second sentence of Article 13. We need the next page for the B/C/S probably.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the interpreters please interpret this. So it's the second sentence that reads as follows: "The minister of the interior is in charge of or has under his control the units of police through the staff of the command of the ministry police forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it, then, Mr. Butler, you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the context of this document, I mean, a change like that does not -- would not change anything that I've previously noted about this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm afraid that again it hasn't been translated properly. There is command and control, RiK, so it is command and control, and there is a difference between the two. So the minister directs, not commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's sufficient for now, and you'll take up the issue during your cross-examination. Yes. Thank you for your patience, Mr. Nicholls. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not -- are we -- is this time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before we get back to another question or two about the MUP, let me ask you something about a question that the Presiding Judge asked you before the break. At pages 29 and 30, His Honour Judge Kwon asked you: Going back to the directive 7/1, were there any other instances other than the case of directive 7/1 where either the command or the commander of the Main Staff issued a further directive which you referred to as a technical expansion, other than the case of 7/1. And you weren't quite sure. I'm just going to see if I can refresh your recollection a bit on that or get your comment on a couple documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 09348, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from the Main Staff. It's from 25th November 1992, titled "Very urgent addition" to operative directive number 4, and then the first line refers to directive 4. Under item 6, providing combat support, that's from directive -- that's the section in directive 4 if we were to bring it up again. "Only basic principles were discussed. In view of the combat situation in all our units, the supplement directive number 4 adds the following." Now this isn't listed as 4.1, but is this -- could you just comment on this document in relation to Judge Kwon's query?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This would be an example of technically amplifying some of the guidance in directive 4. In this particular case, as it notes, only basic principles were discussed and then, you know, either minor or substantial changes occur to a point where they'll issue additional guidance but they don't feel that they have to create a directive 5. This one, if you look at the orders, I mean, it appears in paragraphs 1, 2, and 3, they talk about specific facilities that have to be protected, specific groups that should be set up, preparation of units, but again in paragraph 4, it notes, you know, make these decisions in accordance with directive 4. So it doesn't change directive 4 or the guidance therefore. It just supplements and provides additional technical guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honour? It wasn't on my list, but in light of the conversation, I think it's relevant now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4924, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just in the same line briefly, if I could have P03052.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Main Staff, 14 December 1993, very urgent, this time to the SRK, supplement to directive number 6, and just ask you to comment on what we see here in relation to this topic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I guess it would be the same as my previous comment. We noticed that particularly with respect to paragraph 1, it is detailed. There's a good amount of detail, technical issues, technical details in that paragraph pertaining to various decisions as well as, you know, as you go down on the English language page 1 and perhaps further down on page 2, it talks about various military operations and things of that nature. So again it kind of reinforces what I said earlier, that these are technical supplements to the original base documents. They're not changes to the overall directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Last one, 65 ter number 09475, combat order for carrying out the following combat activities, addition to directive number 6, again from the Main Staff. Just take your time, Mr. Butler, and I'll want to direct you to another page of this afterwards. Just tell me when you're done and we'll go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we have page 2, please, of the English. And I'd also like to show you the last page when you're done.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could have the last page. And there we'll see -- ask your comment in light of what we've been discussing on the section 5 at the bottom: "Secure combat activities pursuant to directive 6," number 6, signed Supreme Commander Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And again, just like the previous documents, these -- particularly with the military operation and tasks assigned they're rather technical, so in this sense, again it amplifies in a technical sense what was basically laid out in directive 6. And this is an example of a good military document in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4925, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Butler. If we could switch gears back to where we were just before the break. I want to show you another document relates -- relating to the use of the MUP in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 1875, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at your tab 14, Mr. Butler, so it's a little out of order. This is dated the 16th of June. It's signed and stamped "President of the Republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic." It's to the government of RS, the ministries, all presidents of Municipal Assemblies, the Main Staff of the VRS. I won't go through it line by line for time. Paragraph 2 states the above-mentioned entities shall bring their activities and behaviour in line with the laws governing a state of imminent threat of war and cites the Official Gazette with this order and other orders that will follow, and then talks about mobilisation and refers to the MUP various places through it. So I won't go through it myself but ask you if you can explain to us the effect or the effect of this order from President Karadzic regarding the use of the MUP in combat.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Simply to the degree that they were not already doing it, this particular order on 16 June 1995, which is now applicable to the entire Republika Srpska, validates that an imminent -- or that an imminent threat of war exists and that all of the organs of the government, which would include the MUP, are to operate in accordance with the various laws that have been written and that were put out in the Official Gazette on 29 November 1994. Specific to the MUP there's a law on the use -- or the Ministry of the Interior in time of imminent threat of war which then references back to some of the prior documents we've looked at which talk about regulating how MUP units are commanded by the military during various operations and how that command and control is effected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4926, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's June 22nd, this order we've just looked at. I want to now move on to July 1995 and Krivaja 95, which you've written extensively about, and then go into the chronology of events which occur after Krivaja 95. You discuss this in the revised narrative, beginning at page 28, and it's footnoted quite a lot in your narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P04481.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is Krivaja 95. And that's at tab 20, Mr. Butler. If we could go first to page 3 of the English, which is also page 3 of the original. In paragraph 2, and we've seen this before but it's from 2nd July: "The command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to operations directive number 7 and 7/1 of the VRS Main Staff and on the basis of the situation in the corps area of responsibility, has the task of carrying out offensive activities with free forces deep in the Drina Corps zone as soon as possible, in order to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, and to reduce them to their urban areas." Further down in paragraph 4 we see the objective for the Drina Corps: "By a surprise attack, to separate and reduce in size the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, to improve the tactical position of the forces in the depth of the area, and to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." And what I'd like to ask you first is this portion I read out refers to direct 7 and 7/1. Can you tell us -- can you comment on this order's basis in those directives and whether this tells us whether 7/1 replaced or supplanted directive 7.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I think as noted in paragraph 2 of this document, the individuals who drafted this particular document understood 7 and 7/1, knew that they were the operative documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Are there any problems with interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Radinovic is not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Me too, but I did not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, we need to fix that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we repeat the last question of yours?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From line 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can Mr. Radinovic hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, he nodded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll read out the last -- I think this is fine, Mr. Butler, and what I'd like to ask you first is this portion I read out refers to directive 7 and 7/1. Can you tell us -- can you comment on this order's basis in those directives and whether this tells us whether 7/1 replaced or supplanted directive 7.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As indicated in paragraph 2 of this particular document, the individual officers who drafted this document, this operations plan, it was their understanding that both directive 7 and 7/1 were the base documents that they were drafting this operations order in accordance with. I don't read this particular passage as an indication that directive 7 no longer existed or was no longer an operative document. I read it as it's written here, which is simply that they're referring to directive 7 and 7/1. The people who drafted this operations order clearly understood the role of both of those documents as a planning basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is signed by the Drina Corps Commander, General Zivanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we go to page 10 of the English, and it would be the last page of the -- that's correct. And the last page of the original. I want to ask you about what this means, the distribution list. We have typed in two copies and delivered to, 1, original in the archive of the Drina Corps command, 2, Main Staff VRS, and then the seven copies made and delivered to these other various units and the IKM of the Drina Corps command. Can you just explain to us what this means where we see this here on the document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, this is the standard distribution, who copies of this operations order would go to, clearly one for the unit archives. You're always going to have a copy of this order at the higher headquarters. And in fact, even before this document was finalised, at some basis the corps would have had to brief the document and the plan to the Main Staff for their approval, and then of course once the plan is finally fixed and all the details are worked out, then copies are sent to the subordinate formations, units, and command posts that would be responsible for implementing the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So with the -- if you could explain to us, would the fact that now this has been signed and stamped and a copy is sent to the Main Staff, does that indicate whether or not the Main Staff has, in fact, approved the plan at this point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Correct, sir. This document, before it was signed, stamped, and finalised, at least a rough draft of this particular document, as well as, you know, a briefing of what the actual plan was intended to be, would have been briefed to the Main Staff subject to their approval prior to General Zivanovic and his officers finalising the plan. So the fact that General Zivanovic has signed this particular document, it has the Drina Corps stamp and it's going out for distribution, the implied behind this is that this plan has already been briefed and approved by the Main Staff. Had it not been so, this plan wouldn't be going out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. In line with that I'd like to show you a map now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is in the map book, 65 ter number 23519. It's map C17, Your Honours, C17 having the English translations on the map. And it should be at e-court pages 28 and 29 for the original and the English. Oh, sorry. Strike that. I've picked the wrong map. E28, Your Honours. I apologise. E29 being the English. At B/C/S -- at e-court pages 35 and 36. And this map is entitled "Decision of the Drina Corps commander for active combat operations, military secret, confidential, Krivaja 95, copy 1."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll ask you to take a look at this map when it comes up, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we could have the English version as well. It should be page 29 -- page 36 of the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we can use only one page, the English version where the legends are interpreted -- translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. That would be good. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's collapse the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, in the meantime, I could give Mr. Butler -- here we go. Yes. And I think -- perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, very simply if we look at this, I don't know if you can read it. It's kind of small, Mr. Butler --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. If we can zoom in on the top left of this Krivaja 95 map, we see: "I approve, Commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic." And if we go down to the bottom, please, on the right, we see the signature of the Drina Corps commander General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So if I can just ask you to tell us what this map and the signatures tell us about the Krivaja 95 operation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And going back to the previous discussion on briefing the Main Staff, while clearly you would have the draft operations order for the staff to review, one of the most effective ways to brief your superior commander about an operation is to do it off of map graphics, and that was the one of the customs of the VRS for particularly large operations. As part of their military practice, the corps and the corps commander would submit this as part of the package, and they would either -- they would physically travel to the Main Staff for this briefing or the Main Staff representatives and the commander would travel to the corps command in cases like this, depending on which one it might be, and there would be a formalised briefing where the plan would be discussed in detail and ultimately proposed by the corps. The custom was as part of their review practice that when the plan was approved by the superior command, it would be noted as such, and you see again on the bottom right-hand corner the submission by the corps commander. And if you go to the top left-hand corner, there's notations there that the plan was approved by the commander, in this case General Ratko Mladic. So this particular document in effect graphically depicts the rather complex JNA staff and planning process that the VRS followed with all of the steps inherent in coming up with a draft operational proposal, flushing it out, putting all the details together, briefing it to the superior command for their comment and ultimately approval, and then disseminating it out to the affected military units that would implement the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just while we're here, it's moving ahead chronologically a bit in the events, but on the right we can see: "Completed. This was Serbian and now it's Serbian! 12 July 1995." Another signature of General Mladic. Can you comment on your interpretation of what that means, the 12 July, Mladic has signed this as completed and that it's now Serbian or remains Serbian.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My understanding of that particular writing at the map was that it was -- this writing or annotation was placed there on the map by General Mladic on the 12th of July, 1995, when they had many of the brigade commanders from the Drina Corps at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters where they were beginning to plan the next military operation against the Zepa enclave. And then as part of that celebratory dinner and planning conference, General Mladic made these notations on the former operation plan map for Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to show you another map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the one I called out earlier, C17, e-court page 22. Again, I think the simplest way is probably to show the version which has the English markings, the translations on the map. This one at the top, if we could blow it up. It states: "Disposition of our enemy and UNPROFOR forces around the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa." On the top right: "Military secret, strictly confidential." And then if we scroll down, under where we see the outlines of the enclaves there are notations on the population, military strength, structure, the ABiH forces, et cetera, as well as UNPROFOR's structure and personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just comment on what this type of map is for prior to Krivaja 95 and -- I'll just ask that to begin with.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I take it from the writing on this map and the topical area of this particular map that this would be one that would be created by the corps intelligence staff. It's what in my military we would call a graphic intelligence estimate. What it depicts and how it relates to Krivaja and Stupcana 95 is it reflects their intelligence estimates of the forces or the -- in this case you include the civilians are right against them inside the enclaves. So this gives an idea of what their understanding was and the accuracy of the information that they had available to them related to the UNPROFOR forces in both the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, the military forces of the 28th Infantry Division within those particular enclaves, as well as overall numbers relating to the civilian population in those particular enclaves. So this is their reflection -- this is their understanding of what the situation was like at least in terms of military and civilian manpower and UN strength for both of these enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And my next question is: If you can, based on all of the work and study you've done on the Srebrenica campaign and events in July 1995, in your assessment, how -- what is the level of accuracy of the estimates relating to the Srebrenica enclave which we see written here regarding the enemy ABiH forces, civilian population, et cetera? And if you have any trouble reading it, I can give you my hard copy.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I've seen this before, so that's not necessary. But it reflects, in my opinion, that the intelligence staff of the Drina Corps had a relatively good picture and an accurate one with respect to the Muslim military forces inside the enclaves, with respect to the UN forces, and the overall population numbers that they use are -- while at the high end, they are consistent with the number ranges that the United Nations themselves were estimating of civilians inside those enclaves. So they had a relatively accurate -- or were receiving relatively accurate information with respect to what they perceived to be the situation in those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that map now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have a time-frame for this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't have an exact one, Your Honour. I'm trying -- it should be something we can figure out. It's just -- clearly it's before Krivaja 95, and I -- but I don't have the -- an exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would -- if I had a take a stab at this, I would say that we're probably looking at March, April, May of 1995, for where these numbers would correspond to what was in the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. We looked at the -- we've looked at directive 4, directive 7, Krivaja 95, and the planning map. I want to now start going quickly through the build-up to the fall of Srebrenica and then the events afterwards and talk a little bit now specifically about reporting and information going up the chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 23684, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 22, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I should point out, Your Honours, to everybody that this is a document I sought leave to add on the 3rd of April notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Given there's no objection, it's granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, and thanks to my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to just tell us a bit about what this -- the significance of this document to you. On the top left we see RS MUP Bijeljina, RDB State Security Department Centre Bijeljina, and the date, 6 July 1995. On the right, for the VRS security department, again signed, and it begins in the first paragraph: "Our source 'Proton' informed us about the contact between political and military leadership in Srebrenica and leadership in Sarajevo that took place early morning 6 July 1995 ..." And I won't read it all, but it is about the Srebrenica representatives asking for a way for Naser Oric in Tuzla to send some troops. In the last paragraph it states: "RDB measures. We will continue to monitor further development of situation in Srebrenica battle-field through our sources and inform you about further developments in due time."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please provide the reference for interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the bottom last paragraph that begins "RDB measures." And I'll wait a minute. "We verbally informed the representatives of the VRS OB about the said information source Merkur and personal observations of the operative information reliable." And I think there's actually a typo that I read out, I'm sorry. In the first paragraph where it says "our source 'Proton'," in fact that should be Merkur as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So could you please tell us what this document indicates about sharing or first of all about monitoring of military events by the RDB.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I guess to step back one, within the context of at least the enclaves in Eastern Bosnia, it was not just the military intelligence and security apparatus that was collecting information on them. The MUP Ministry of Interior was impacted by those enclaves as well and collected information on them. So effectively within the context of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska, there are three chains of information that exists by which information relating to the enclaves are being passed up and down the various communications chain. First you have the army reporting on issues; second, that you have the police reporting on issues; and the third is that you have the State Security Service reporting on issues. And as indicated in this particular document, they are doing so in co-operation with each other. The RDB is not keeping information from the military. The military is not keeping information from the RDB. They're not keeping information from the police. So all three of these intelligence collectors, so to speak, are -- are working in co-operation with each other to ensure that everyone has the most accurate and common picture of the events as they are occurring. So from that perspective, the -- the intelligence apparatuses of the state are working as they should. They're also doing the second part of intelligence which is they're reporting that up to the various chains of command. So they're ensuring that their higher levels within both the military and the Ministry of the Interior are informed of the things that they are learning as well and what they are telling the VRS and what the VRS is telling state security. So this particular document is an excellent example of that type of co-operation between the army and the MUP with respect to obtaining and passing what they believe to be important information about the opposing military forces in the enclave as the operation is beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4927, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. If I could now have 23658, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at your next tab, Mr. Butler. Just same topic. This is from the RS -- this is headed RS MUP, RDB state security department, to Republika Srpska deputy minister of the interior personally, and RS MUP public security department personally. And it's dated 6th of June at the top but we see immediately that it's discussing the 6th of July. First of all, do you recall who the deputy minister of the interior was at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I believe in June and July of 1995 it was Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the head of public security, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I always get him and the head of the RDB confused. I think Kajic is RDB and the name is escaping me for that. I'm sure we'll see it in another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Can I just remind you? Is it Karisik? Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That's -- that's the name, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So this going to them and it states: "Early in the morning of 6th July 1995 representatives," I'm reading from the top, "of the political and military leadership of Srebrenica established radio contact with the leadership in Sarajevo." The Srebrenica representatives wanted some way to be found for Naser Oric to return to their area urgently and it again discusses three units, as did the previous document we looked at, which was dated also 6th July. Could you just comment on this document as to what you started talking about a moment ago about information through various branches being sent up the chain.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Within the context of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska, information was reported to the highest levels at least on a daily basis by the Main Staff in what they would call their daily combat activities report, which went to the Supreme Command, and from the MUP side they also published not only daily but as necessary intelligence information reports to their leadership. In the case of the MUP, it would be the minister of the interior, Mr. Kovac, who again is a member of the Supreme Command body. So these particular documents, you know, reflect the fact that there was an established mechanism, formal mechanism, by which information about not only Srebrenica but the entirety of the Republika Srpska and the armed conflict that was occurring and those issues from both a military as well as a political perspective were transmitted to the highest levels of the Republika Srpska leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4928, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to continue to move chronologically now, so we'll come back to some of these reporting issues later as it works in. We were just at 6th July. I'd like to now show you P04484. This is an intercept that we've looked at -- it's not an intercept, excuse me. It's a dictaphone audio recording of a conversation between President Karadzic and General Zivanovic that I believe you hadn't seen before we met and talked about these issues this weekend.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is correct. That's the first time I'd seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is at your tab 26, Mr. Butler. Looking through this tape -- and it's not dated but we'll look at some documents later that may help explain approximately when this occurred. I won't read the entire document out, but President Karadzic asks at mid point down the first page in the English: [As read] "... so it looks that immediate task is completed, right?" The answer from the Drina Corps commander Zivanovic is: "It is." And President Karadzic asks: "Are Sise" - if I pronounce it correctly - "ours?" And then Zivanovic says: "They are." And there's a little bit of discussion about that. I'll stop there. What does that refer to, Sise, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: There's a series of hilltops that geographically on the map are -- are south of Srebrenica, the town, that are essentially along the road from Zeleni Jadar to Srebrenica. The main axis of the attack was from Zeleni Jadar to Srebrenica. These hills had a -- of course a slang nickname that were referred to by the local soldiers and of course the leaders knew it as well, but militarily, it was recognised that for any attack into or towards the actual town of Srebrenica to succeed, that the Bosnian Serb military forces that were attacking were going to have to take and control these hilltops. So essentially what they were referring to is the fact that their forces have achieved those initial objectives and that they're controlling those terrain features.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It might be clearer let me bring up -- bring up a map and have you, if you can, show us where these three features are. This would be D20 in the map book, e-court page 26, I think is a good page.
