Now, my only interest in the map at this point, Mr. Butler, when it comes up is for you to just show us where these three elevations are, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment. Translators didn't, neither we, didn't see the whole document in Serbian version so to follow what is presented to witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're referring to the audio recording?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yeah, but Serbian version is not scrolled as according to what you've been talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, what is your question about? In English translation says, "Are the tits ours," but you refer to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, that is what I'm referring to, Your Honours. The Serbian word is "Sise." That's what I was reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you said in B/C/S when you referred to "tits."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. Yes. It's the three mountains that are referred to as "the three tits" that are at the Zeleni Jadar area, to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So now you understood, Mr. Karadzic? Yes. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We just need the map up for Mr. Butler. And that's 65 ter number 23519, e-court page 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think it's kind of towards the bottom right, Mr. Butler. Is that the part we should blow-up?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The lower right-hand side of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just tell us how -- how much you need it enlarged.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That should suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed, Mr. Nicholls, is this a separate map or part of a --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's an excerpt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So which is zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm just using it for the purpose of him showing where these mountains are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You'll note that I've circled in red three corresponding hilltops which are what colloquially they referred to as "the three tits." Militarily or geographically you can see that they control or they dominate the road from Zeleni Jadar in the south towards Srebrenica in the north, and that before you could launch any effective attack toward Srebrenica, you had to secure those three terrain features. So that was a key early military objective for the attacking forces of the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would tender this marked segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably it may be more useful if we zoom in further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then let's ask the witness to mark it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that we can see the features more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, just zoom in that part. Further. We can zoom in once again so that we can read the numbers even. Yes. I think that's sufficient. Please wait. Probably you need to push the button for the colour or something. No, no. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So those are the ... [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask to give this a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be Exhibit P4929.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now if we could go back to the audio recording, P04484, that we were looking at a moment ago. And that's at tab 26, Mr. Butler. And to save time, I will just read a bit before it comes up. Lower down after Mr. Karadzic says: [As read] "That's good. We shouldn't give Sise, the tits, at any cost." And there's some laughter. And then President Karadzic says: "So, what's going on? There were some blue ones with us, right? "Pardon? "There are the blue ones on our side, right? "They should be treated well. "Properly, properly." And then a discussion how there were no losses. Based on what you know was going on at about the time that this operation took place which seized the Sise, these three elevations, what would that conversation about the blues refer to, do you believe?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In this context they're already taking custody of some of the UN soldiers who were at check-points which the UN was observing and actually had on some of these heights, and rather than fall back through the battle-field area which they deemed to be too dangerous, a number of these UN detachments essentially came over to the Bosnian Serb side and were taken into custody by the Bosnian Serbs. So I believe that in this particular context what they are discussing is the confirmation that President Karadzic is aware that, you know, they -- that the Army of Republika Srpska has custody of some UN peacekeepers who are there and is noting that they should be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we go to the next page in the English. Sorry, it must be -- I may have a different version on the first page then. Back to the first page of the English. Yes, first page of the English, please. If we could look at the -- towards the bottom where it states: [As read] "Fine. So I can't give any of the," and then there's a word we can't hear, "to you. Everything is taken and only if you need any large ones, it should be checked through the Main Staff. I know that there is some and where it is, so we could probably reinforce you a little." Zivanovic: "We will also need that." Karadzic: "Pardon?" "That will also be ... needed." President Karadzic: "All right, call the Main Staff up there, and I know that it came in, and you can call me via Barijera and we could talk and reinforce." And then a little bit further down, Zivanovic says: "They're escaping that way. I've urged Gvero up there that the Milici and Bratunac radio stations be put at a higher intellectual level, so to speak, and to start working on it a bit through the media. I don't mean soft persuasion, not persuasion."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, first of all I'm going to look at some documents in a minute, but based on your study of this document that we saw this weekend, what is President Karadzic saying to General Zivanovic about reinforcements and calling up there to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There -- even with the forces that they already had available to them, they already knew that they were looking to get more combat forces, and one of the options that was out there was potentially to use some of the MUP forces that were deployed in other areas of the battle-field to be reallocated to the Krivaja 95 operation. And in fact if you look several days later, that is in fact exactly what happens. So I mean in this context, President Karadzic is reminding General Zivanovic he has a general awareness of the overall situation, he knows what's going on, saying, Look, if you need those additional forces, you know, begin the process of doing that through the Main Staff and we may be able to get them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And could we go now to the next page in English, please. And continuing the conversation that we just talked about, about the media and the radio stations, President Karadzic said: "All right, have someone prepare instructions for the journalists and I will approve them, the minister for ..." And Zivanovic says: "I told this to Gvero and hope it will be carried out in that sense." And then a minute later President Karadzic says: "All right, just tell Krle that I can't get to him right now, well, the entire MUP is engaged. I really don't have -- these from Zvornik are the last reserves of these in Sarajevo, at Treskavica, in fact at Trnovo. Zivanovic says: "Yes." President Karadzic says: "So there is no other way. You have to go with your own forces." First of all, do you know from your study of this what the nickname Krle, whose nickname -- who that refers to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's the nickname for General Radislav Krstic who at this time is the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps but is physically located now at the Drina Corps forward command post south of Srebrenica where he's actively directing Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then just a little bit further down, Karadzic towards the end of the conversation says: "All right, General, full speed ahead. Tell Krstic order them to go full steam ahead." And Zivanovic replies: "We are working pretty much according to plan and it's going well, and thank God that we don't have any losses. That's the key, especially in these first attacks." And then there's some more. If you could just comment what this conversation we see tells us about the Supreme Commander's ability during combat operations to consult with corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, I believe this particular document is illustrative of several points. The most obvious one is that the Supreme Commander is not limited to receiving formal reports about the military situation in any particular area of the battle-field. He has the physical ability and obviously in this particular case chose to exercise it to directly call the corps commander of the corps that's conducting this operation, General Zivanovic, to get a situational update and to directly pass on instructions through General Zivanovic to his subordinate which is General Krstic. So in that particular sense, it reflects the fact that President Karadzic as the Supreme Commander of the armed forces is engaged in this process. It also reflects the fact that he has a detailed awareness of not only what's happening on the ground at Srebrenica, because he has chosen to inquire, but also he has detailed awareness of military operations in other areas. In this respect, he's talking about the MUP forces deployed at Sarajevo, Treskavica, Trnovo. And he has enough of a knowledge base to know that it would be problematic at that particular point to have to pull out MUP forces from one axis to reinforce the Drina Corps in another one. He's not saying that it can't be done or that a way wouldn't be found, but he's not making any knee-jerk reactions. He has an appreciation of the various risks on other areas of the battle-field and is managing those risks. So it reflects to me an individual who is suitably engaged in what's happening within the context of the conflict at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to go quickly through a few documents that are all dated 8 July 1995 and just see if it gives us some context to the phone conversation -- or the conversation, I should say, that we just talked about and to help date it. The first one is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we do so, just out of curiosity --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- if you could help us as regards who or what Barijera is, when Mr. Karadzic said to inform him via Barijera on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And I can't, unfortunately. I don't believe I know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could just have one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 23465, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 27, Mr. Butler, of your binder. This is a Drina Corps command 8 July 1995 urgent regular combat report to the Main Staff. Time stamp is processed at 19.36, and if we could look at page 2, requests made by General Zivanovic. Paragraph 9. "Due to the possibility of enemy attacks in the north-western part of the front," I'll skip a couple words, "please engage MUP forces from Zvornik, their 1st Company, through the RS MUP as reserve forces for the 1st Birac Infantry Brigade on standby to intervene along the endangered axis." Again, signed by General Zivanovic. I'd just ask you if you can comment on this paragraph and its relation, if any, to the conversation we looked at.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It talks about the 8 July conversations -- or not conversation, but it talks about the situation on 8 July, the recognition that they're receiving information that there may be other attacks against the Drina Corps in part to relieve pressure on Srebrenica. In this particular thing they talk about the access from Kalesija, Kladanj and Olovo, and they're already talking about the possibility of a MUP -- the 1st MUP Company from Zvornik, which is down at Trnovo, to at least put them on standby to have to deploy to these areas if the situation dictates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And is this a request -- you talked about earlier the way use of the MUP forces worked. Is this a request, I think you used the phrase "to get the process started" or something like that, to engage the MUP? Is this the right way to do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this would be an example of the correct way to do that. This report would go to the Main Staff. The Main Staff, having a better view of the entire battle-field, would be able to sit down and make determinations as to what the overall battle-field situation was, where these forces or if these forces could be redeployed or made available and what risks they would assume in doing so, and would those risks be worth the gain that they anticipate. So this is part of, you know, that overall military planning process that's always ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd tender that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4930, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Moving along to another 8 July document, Mr. Butler. This is at your tab 28, P04482, please. It's a Drina Corps IKM Pribicevac urgent interim combat report. And I won't read it out to save time, but if you could take a look at paragraphs 2 and 5 and tell us if this 8 July document relates to the conversation between Mr. Karadzic -- President Karadzic at the time and General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again they're talking about in this particular interim report, which is drafted by General Krstic who is at the forward command post in Pribicevac, where this interim report is updating both the command of the Drina Corps and the Main Staff on the overall combat situation, and again as part of that, you know, it dovetails in with the conversation that we heard previously with respect to General Zivanovic and President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We see in paragraph 2: "Our forces seized control over the key installations on this axis including the Tri Sise," the three tits. And in paragraph 5 a reference to UNPROFOR forces who surrendered, seven of them, to the VRS because they felt they needed to be protected from Muslim forces. It says they were sent to Bratunac. Is that -- does that connect to the conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene once again? It seems to me that seven were sent to Potocari. That's the first part of the sentence, to their base, to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. There's another reference to seven to Bratunac, but the document says what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is a document that has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Very quickly, if I could have 23464, please, again 8 July. This is from General Zivanovic to the Main Staff, to the assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just recalling in the conversation there was a discussion where Zivanovic said, "I already told that to Gvero," and spoke about using radio stations in Milici and Bratunac. This document from Zivanovic to the assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs personally at the Main Staff, who is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The -- the actual assistant commander at the Main Staff would be General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I admit this, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4931, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Finally in this same -- to round up these documents from 8 July, D02099.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 30, Mr. Butler. This is the Main Staff of the army of the RS, 8 July, very urgent report to the various corps and command posts but, at the top, to the president of the Republika Srpska. If we could go to page 3 of the English. It's also page 3 of the Serbian original. Paragraph 6. I think it's kind of self-evident, but again if you can tell us where we see here on the part of the front towards Srebrenica, "the Tri Sise feature was seized by us." We saw the conversation with Mr. Karadzic. Can you tell us what this shows about reporting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It just reflects the consistency of the reporting by the military of the information up the chain, up the reporting chain. As it initially came from the forward command post, the IKM, through the Drina Corps command to the Main Staff and then is being reported by the Main Staff to not only its corps and other army elements, but for the benefit primarily of the president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now moving on to the next day, 9 July. I'd like to show you D02080, Drina Corps IKM, Pribicevac, very urgent interim combat report from Chief of Staff Radislav Krstic. It's got handwritten time stamp of -- not stamp but handwritten time of 23.20, received, on the bottom. And if you could just take us through this, your knowledge of the chronology of the events of the fall of Srebrenica. What is Krstic reporting on here? What's happened? Where is the VRS now, the night of 9 July, in terms of the objectives in directive 7 and Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In this particular context of time, what is happening by the end of the evening here of 9 July is that despite what they have described as significant resistance by enemy forces, that the VRS has now taken all of the relevant necessary terrain features to the south of Srebrenica which would not only allow them to move north now into the town of Srebrenica, but as they've also noted, we've taken additional terrain features which serve to physically separate the known smuggling and communication routes between Srebrenica and Zepa or -- essentially cutting the military communications routes between the two enclaves. General Krstic is essentially saying, We've achieved all of the initial objectives laid out in Krivaja 95, and as a result, the conditions are now set for us to continue to advance and again carry out a decisive attack towards Srebrenica. So I mean he's -- he's relatively optimistic about what is -- what he's accomplished so far and is making sure that the Drina Corps command as well as the Main Staff are aware of the fact that, you know, as he sees it, the initial and potentially the hardest phase of the operation is completed, is done successfully, and now the stage is set for the next follow-on, which is to really push towards the urban area of Srebrenica as far as he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'd like to look now at P02276. Again from 9 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the next tab in your binder, Mr. Butler. Main Staff to the president for information. To the Drina Corps IKM, where we just saw General Krstic was. And to Generals Gvero and Krstic personally, it states. The Chamber has even this before so I won't go through every line of it, but it starts off: "The President of Republika Srpska has been informed of successful combat operations around Srebrenica by units of the Drina Corps and that they have achieved results which enable them to occupy the very town of Srebrenica. The President of the Republic is satisfied with the results of combat operations throughout Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation of operations for the take-over of Srebrenica, disarming of Muslim terrorist gangs, and complete demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave." And then the president has ordered to ensure that UNPROFOR members and Muslim civilians are protected and guaranteed safety, et cetera, and to obey the Geneva Conventions and not burn down homes. There are stamps here for 2350 hours on 9 July. The other stamp we saw was 23.20. I would just like your view on this document, what it indicates about Karadzic as Supreme Commander at this time, July 1995, receiving reports from the field and being able to make decisions and issue orders based on those reports, if you can.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, certainly within the time-frame, this is a classic example of two orders passing each other in the night about the same time. You can infer that at some juncture prior to him actually writing out his interim report, General Krstic has at least verbally briefed his commander, the Drina Corps, and the Main Staff, about the military situation and the opportunities that are available. So that even before they receive his interim report officially on paper, they have enough information to go forward and brief the Supreme Commander as to the ongoing military situation, the current opportunities that are available to the army as a result of successful operations to date, and to, you know, receive guidance as to what should be the next objective or, in this particular context, the final objective. So even though when you look at the time stamps of the documents coming back and forth, it's clear that there's a very detailed discussion going on between the military commanders on the ground and the Main Staff, and that they're comfortable enough with the overall picture that they brief the president of the republic about what opportunities are out there, what are the potential military objectives that could be taken, and in fact this particular document reflects that the Main Staff did that and that they received the authorisation from the president of the republic to actually move forwards and occupy the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir -- sorry. Mr. Butler. I apologise. If you could help us understand the structure in which this kind of order is sent out -- why -- why General Tolimir is sending out this order. And where were General Mladic -- Mladic or General Milovanovic? Why were they skipped, if you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- well, in the case of General Milovanovic, I won't say that he was skipped, but certainly we can account for his absence based on the fact that he was dealing with issues in the Krajina during this period. I don't know that in the case of General Mladic, whether General Mladic was personally present at the Supreme Command briefing General Mladic [sic] and that what you're looking at is Mladic calling General Tolimir back at the Main Staff headquarters to relay the order to General Krstic or whether or not General Mladic was not physically present because he was en route to somewhere else, but General Tolimir as the senior officer there was doing in effect -- representing General Mladic. This particular document doesn't lay it specifically out that -- that framework of who attended that meeting. So I mean, I can't infer too much about whether or not various military officials were or were not skipped. I don't -- from my historical research on this particular document and everything else, there's nothing irregular about it in the sense that it's General Tolimir relaying the message to General Krstic and General Gvero, who we know on the 9th of July is at the forward command post. I don't know again where General Mladic was and whether he was the person physically briefing General Karadzic -- I'm sorry, President Karadzic, whether he was en route somewhere else, and how these orders were relayed through General -- from General -- or from the Supreme Commander to General Tolimir. So I mean, it's just not implicit in the actual document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It might be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time. We will break for an hour and resume at 1.30. In the meantime, if you could excuse yourself for a moment, there's one thing I would like to deal with in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Butler, if you could go to tab 34 in your binder. That's 65 ter 23686, a document from 10th of July, another RDB Bijeljina document signed by that centre chief, Goran Radovic. And I'm just going to ask some more questions now as we move along chronologically about information being shared and processed. This document has handwritten on the top right: "For the VRS security department," signed by Dragan somebody. We don't have the last name. More RDB intelligence. The first paragraph states: "Please be informed that the VRS units deployed in Srebrenica battle-field further moved the front line reaching the line Pribicevac Olivine, Bojna," and then some elevations, "and Pusmulici in the late evening hours of 9 July ..." And states at the bottom: "We will continue to monitor further developments of situation in Srebrenica battle-field through our sources and inform you about these further developments in due time." Now before I ask you a question about that if I could have 65 ter 23687 up and I'll ask you a question about both documents. That's tab 35, Mr. Butler, the next one. This document is from the RS MUP state security department Sarajevo, signed by head of RDB Dragan Kijac, to the deputy minister of the interior personally, and we established that that was Tomo Kovac. And in the first paragraph it begins: "On 9 July this year, the army -- VRS units on the Srebrenica battle-field shifted the front line," and contains the same information as we saw in the one from Goran Radovic of the Bijeljina centre, "up." So if you look at these two documents together, can you again just comment on what it says to you, including the reference in the first document that it's to be shared with VRS security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe this reflects a positively functioning information and intelligence chain where information is being collected at the lower levels. It is being disseminated up to the various chains to the leadership levels, first to the head of the RDB, which then uses the same information to send it to the minister, in this case the deputy minister of the interior and the head of the public security department. And it notes in the initial document that the information is also being shared with the army. So it reflects the continuing close co-ordination and co-operation that the intelligence collection and reporting units or agencies have at the lowest level and rising upwards through the information chain on making sure that all parties have a detailed view of what is happening and, again, more importantly, making sure that that accurate detailed view is being transmitted to their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender those two documents, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They will be admitted as Exhibits P4932 and P4933 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like to look at another MUP document from 10 July, the same day. This is at tab 38, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P02992. That may be the wrong number. That's the correct document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you talk about this in your revised narrative at pages 32 to 33, paragraph 3.20, and you footnote it in your brigade command report at footnotes 140, 141, and 142, and in the revised narrative at 194, 195, and some other places. I won't read them all because it's footnoted quite a lot. This is the 10 July order type-signed by Tomo Kovac. Pursuant to the order of the Supreme Commander of the RS and in order to crush enemy offences being carried out from the safe area of Srebrenica. I won't ask you any specific questions right now. I'd like you to just explain the significance of this document which you included in your reports.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In this context, the significance is reflected at the very beginning where it talks about, you know, an order -- based on an order from the Supreme Commander of the armed forces and for the purpose of defeating, crushing, the enemy offensive from the Srebrenica protected zone, a series of orders are being given out by Mr. Kovac. This dovetails with the provisions of the Republika Srpska Law on the Interior Ministry during time of imminent threat of war or state of war, where it discusses the fact that when the MUP units are going to be used by army forces, then it's the MUP that decides what forces they are and to what degree that they will be resubordinated to the army and under what circumstances. So they're particularly identifying which units will be pulled out from which battle-field areas, who is going to be in command of those particular units, when they're supposed to depart, where they're supposed to go, and in paragraph 5, when they arrive at that location, who that they're supposed to report to. In this case, General Krstic, the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we see in here in paragraph 2 that one of the units -- well, the units are the 2nd Special Detachment -- the 2nd Sekovici Detachment of the Special Police, the 1st Company of the PJP unit from Zvornik SJB, and then the mixed company of the joint RSK Serbian and RS MUP forces. But speaking of the 1st Company from Zvornik, can you link that at all to the telephone -- to the conversation we saw a couple of days earlier between President Karadzic and General Zivanovic and the subsequent request by General Zivanovic for the 1st Company from Zvornik to assist?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that that's the same unit, so of the number of military -- of Special Police Units that they're getting, certainly one of them is the unit that they specifically asked for, the 1st PJP Company from Zvornik CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in fact -- and we'll see some more documents later, but based on your research and understanding, did Commander Borovcanin and these units come and assist on the Srebrenica battle-field or the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They ultimately arrived in the Bratunac area in the late afternoon of the 11th of July, 1995. So by then the town of Srebrenica had already been captured by the VRS forces advancing from Zeleni Jadar, but, you know, the 1st Sekovici Detachment did arrive, the 1st PJP Company did arrive. The one company from Jahorina training centre did arrive. The one unit that did not appear to come down there to participate was the joint MUP forces of the Republic of Serb Krajina, Serbia and the Republika Srpska. There's no evidence that that particular mixed company ever showed up at Potocari on the 11th with the other formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could quickly look now at P02242, e-court page 89 in English and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is at your tab 36, Mr. Butler. And this is President Karadzic's appointment diary for 10 July 1995, when it comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we need page 89, if I have my numbers right. There we go. And we see the entry at 1700, Dragan Kijac and Milenko Karisik meeting with the president the same day that this MUP order was issued sending the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that this is the head of state security and head of public security meeting with Mr. Karadzic that day at that time, can you comment on what this tells you, if anything, about the communications of information from the field up to the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that this calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was actually think the very same thing, and also believe that this is really beyond the expertise of this witness. There's nothing more that he can add as a military analyst to what you can already infer from the evidence, and I don't believe that this is a necessary part of his expertise in which his opinion would be helpful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the MUP was part of armed forces of the Serb -- Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's absolutely true, but you now have before you the fact that these two people met with Dr. Karadzic and that there'd been this communication and what can he tell you any more than what -- he's inferring just the same the thing that you can infer. There's nothing from your military expertise that would inform you or assist you about. It's just speculating and drawing inferences that the Chamber should be drawing itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I hear your position, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I disagree, Your Honour. As you say, it's a member -- these -- the MUP is a branch of the armed forces which President Karadzic as Supreme Commander commands. These two men are the head of two branches, the state security and public security of the MUP. It's no different than if Mr. -- President Karadzic at this time is meeting with a VRS subordinate, such as he meets later with Petar Skrbic, for example, during this time period, and he's communicating as we've seen with other -- and we will see with General Gvero during this time period. So I think it's completely within this expert witness's remit to talk about the significance -- I haven't asked him to say what they talked about or speculate on the topic, but to talk about whether the fact that the Supreme Commander not only receives reports, calls commanders in the field, but actually meets in his office with his subordinates during critical periods of a military campaign at the same time that important military orders are being issued has any significance to the way communication and command is exercised, because probably in some cases commanders don't meet in person in their offices with subordinates in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand your point but the issue is whether we need the assistance of this witness to interpret this event. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will hear from Mr. Nicholls, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to say I don't know what the answer will be, but it's conceivable that personal meetings with commanders are part of a rubric that the witness can comment on that adds something to the picture in addition to other forms of communication through phone, radio, or written reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just in brief reply. The example of Petar Skrbic is an excellent one, because you have a similar situation. Petar Skrbic meets with Dr. Karadzic during this time period. We're fortunate enough to have his testimony here, and he testified that he never discussed anything about Srebrenica during that time. So to ask for comments for this -- from this witness is just the kind of speculation that you don't need any help in making. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Butler hasn't come as a fact witness, and the Chamber can draw its own conclusion on these facts, so we don't think we need his assistance in interpreting this event. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, moving up to -- just moving quickly to 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And to try to save a little bit of time, I'll just bring these intercepts up quickly. Could I have P40629.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 42, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, P04629. My mistake. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an intercepted conversation between General Gvero and President Karadzic at 16.23. And do you recall -- I won't ask questions about it now, but do you recall having seen and read this intercept before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in a different iteration. I am familiar with this particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now could I have P04630.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's at tab 43, Mr. Butler. Twenty minutes later, so at approximately 16.43, on the same day. Now, in the first intercept we saw General Gvero saying everything's going according to plan, don't worry, and in this one we see - I won't go through it because of time - the conversation where we can only see what General Gvero is saying. [As read] "President, Serbian silver, the Serbian church, the Serbian flag. But they don't have a reason for it. The Turks probably shot at them, if they shot at all at UNPROFOR. They are in the air again. They are setting up again like before. Good, President, good luck." The last one in the series, P04633, just about the same time on 11 July, 16.41. This intercept in which we can hear President Karadzic: "They're not allowed to attack us." The unidentified person: "They have no reason probably." Some of the same words. And Karadzic says: "Yes, I believe so, but if they start diving, shoot them down." Now what I'd like to ask you is about what this tells you, from your military background, about the level of communications available to the Supreme Commander to contact a member -- one of his generals in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Putting the three together, there are three general thematics that they're discussing. The first one is the acknowledgment that the VRS has captured Srebrenica. They're talking about who, if anybody, has been firing on UNPROFOR. And then the third issue that they are discussing is the fact that, again, having been previously attacked by NATO Air Forces over the Srebrenica enclave, and I think those air attacks went in at about 1300, 1400 on the 11th of July, they are noting that there is still aircraft flying over the enclave and instructions being passed what to do if they're attacked again. In light of the obvious political sensitivity of all three issues, it's not surprising that the president of the republic would be personally inquiring as to what the situation is, what the army was doing or intended to do about things, and telling General Gvero what instructions should be followed. It reflects that when it mattered and when it was deemed important to the supreme leader or the Supreme Commander in this case, he wasn't shy about directly reaching out to his subordinate military officers in order to get an accurate picture of what was happening and to ensure that they understood what his guidance was under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move to P04450. We won't go through all of the VRS Main Staff reports to the president, the daily reports during this period, but this one I'd like to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at your tab 46, Mr. Butler. And if we look at page 3 of the English and of the Serbian, we can see the section on the Drina Corps zone of responsibility. At the bottom of subsection (a), The enemy, it states: "In the Srebrenica enclave the enemy has been putting up fierce resistance to VRS units. The NATO Air Force has been pounding our forces in the following sectors," et cetera. "An interim report on the situation in Srebrenica and the NATO Air Force is forthcoming." (B), Situation in the corps. If we can turn the page. "The corps units are in a state of full combat readiness. The main forces are being used to mount a persistent defence and part of these forces are involved in offensive operations around the Srebrenica enclave. In the course of the day, our forces entered the town of Srebrenica," and it says that more reports will be coming. This is from General Miletic. He's at the Main Staff. Can you just discuss here the portion I've read out, the reporting on the entry of the forces into Srebrenica, and comment on the accuracy and working of the VRS chain of information up to the president.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: This is a reflection again of the fact that the president is being kept adequately informed by at least one of the three existing reporting chains that -- that are documented, in this case the military reporting chain. We have an opportunity, when we look at the documents, to see that the reporting is going from the lower military units to the intermediate units to the Main Staff, it's being then processed and it's going directly to, you know, the president of the Republika Srpska, and it's consistent with what the president of the Republika Srpska is hearing from other individuals associated with the army, for example, that discussion with General Gvero. It's a reflection that at this particular point this reporting chain is working just as it's supposed to be working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, since we're not going to go through every single one for July 1995, if you've reviewed them, can you just tell us generally your view of the reporting during this month these -- and I'm speaking specifically about these VRS Main Staff reports which go up every day to the president, since we won't look at every single one.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: From my review of them in previous situations, they reflect a consistent and conscientious effort by the military to accurately report on the facts from lower levels to higher echelon levels to the Main Staff and ultimately to the president of the republic. There's details -- obviously, as you go higher up the chains, you know, the smaller details tend to get left out because individuals deem that, you know, that's not newsworthy to the President of Republika Srpska. But when you look at the body of reports from the forward operating units to the highest levels, I mean you can certainly see the consistency of the reporting. As we call it in the US military, the major muscle movements are all the same. It's just a question of how much minutia from any particular unit is deemed valuable enough so that the president of the republic needs to know of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to now bring up D202055. This is the decision on the appointment of the civilian commissioner for the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're still going in chronological order. It's 11 July 1995, signed by President Karadzic. This is footnoted in your Srebrenica revised narrative, footnotes 199 to 201. It's at tab 47, Mr. Butler. And what I wanted to ask you about was paragraph 4 specifically. It states, and I'll read it while it's coming up in the English -- oh, there it is. "The commissioner shall ensure that all civilian and military organs treat all citizens who participated in combat against the Army of Republika Srpska as prisoners of war and ensure that the civilian population can freely choose where they will live or move to." And can you just comment about what it says here in paragraph 4? Who's responsible at this point for the treatment of prisoners of war under the regulations and practice as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I don't read -- I mean, in short, I don't read paragraph 4 to reflect that the president of the republic has given Miroslav Deronjic the responsibility for the treatment of all prisoners of war. His job is to ensure that civilian and military organisations are treating them as such in the prescribed manner, but he ultimately isn't responsible for that. The prisoners initially are in the custody of the military or the police units that capture them. How the prisoners are going to be detained, the protocols, and who they ultimately belong to within the context of the state of the Republika Srpska are well defined in the applicable regulations as to the Law of Armed Conflict on the former SFRY which the JNA -- or which the VRS adopted. So again, while Mr. Deronjic's job may have been to, you know, monitor what was happening with these individual units and presumably if they were not being complied with report that up to Karadzic as the president of the republic, Miroslav Deronjic of himself would not have had the authority to tell the military units or the police units that they had to stop or do certain things with them. I mean, that authority remained vested with the appropriate military and police organs as part of the armed forces and ultimately with President Karadzic as the head of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now moving into 12 July, and we'll start moving a little bit quicker, I think, through the days. I'd like to look at 65 ter 21950.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at tab 51, Mr. Butler. This is the RS Ministry of the Interior police force staff Pale order from the next day, 12 July 1995. "In order to take over urgent task of mopping up the terrain in the Srebrenica sector, I hereby order: "1 --" I'll wait, for the interpreters, until the document comes up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told, Mr. Nicholls, that it hasn't been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me. Just while we're waiting for the document to come up, I just want to note that I'll need five minutes at the end of this session to raise something in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] All right. I'll come back to that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll come back to that one in a minute. Hopefully. Let's look at another 12 July document. This is P04680. It's an intercept of a conversation on 12 July, 0735 hours. Actually, I think this should not be broadcast perhaps, but I can read the main text. It's an intercept of a conversation between Krstic and Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, first question: Was there a Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic was the chief of transportation services for the Drina Corps in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at this point General Krstic is Chief of Staff still; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just tell us your understanding of what this document is -- the significance of it at 7.35 in the morning of the 12th of July, before the last Hotel Fontana meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before Mr. Butler answers the question, I'm not sure whether we should not broadcast this. I think -- I was told that this is admitted publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In that that case, I apologise, Your Honour. We can broadcast. I just wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Well, at this point in time this particular intercept discussion is relating to the knowledge of both parties, General Krstic and Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic, where they're talking about buses from various locations, various municipalities, are going to be arriving at the Bratunac area at a certain time, and in this context by 1700, and they're going to make sure they arrive and all of the other associated work that needs to be done with them is done. There are a number of other documents that are in my report which reflect earlier orders from the Main Staff and requested from the Main Staff to the Ministry of Defence where they're requesting the mobilisation of buses from various municipalities to go to Bratunac at this time. So these orders are going out sometime during the late evening hours of the 11th, early morning hours of the 12th of July, 1995, and so this conversation kind of is on the back end of that process where you now have the local military individuals, General Krstic and Colonel Krsmanovic discussing the issues of inbound buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I think I can go back to 65 ter 21950. And that's at tab 51, Mr. Butler. All right. This is again type-signed by Deputy Minister Tomislav or Tomo Kovac, dated 12 July 1995, very urgent, to the command centre for the breeding and training of police dogs. "In order to take over urgent task of mapping up the terrain in the Srebrenica sector, I hereby order: "1. Urgently dispatch all available guides with police dogs to the Srebrenica sector. "2. Upon arrival in Srebrenica contact Ljubisa Borovcanin, deputy commander of the Special Police Brigade who commands the police forces in Srebrenica, and make arrangements on what to do next." And can you just tell us at this point, 12 July 1995, the order from Tomo Kovac assigning these units, can you comment on what that shows about the way MUP forces are being deployed at this time in this operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We know from other documents that at this time there are at least the three MUP companies that are there by the afternoon or early evening hours of the 11th of July. The commander of those forces was Mr. Borovcanin. The implied issue behind this is that for whatever reason Mr. Borovcanin believed that he required to have these dogs from the training centre, he made the formal request to the police staff and that request was granted. So a functional chain of command in this case. A subordinate makes a request. It goes to the higher staff, in this case the police staff, and in the name of the minister of the interior, the order is given and these dog guide units are, in fact, sent to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P02995, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at tab 54, Mr. Butler. Another MUP document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we ask Mr. Nicholls to show us the entire page. Hopefully there is a receipt stamp indicating when Kovac received it and the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My original copy doesn't have any time stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been reminded. May I tender 21950?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4934, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you take a look at this document, Mr. Butler, it's from the RS Minister of the Interior, or the office of the minister, 12 July. Again from Deputy Minister Tomo Kovac. This one does have a time at the top, 0235 hours. Again, very urgent. It's to the Zvornik public security centre chief. And just if you recall, do you remember who was the chief in Zvornik in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That would be Mr. Vasic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what we see here is that Tomo Kovac is sending a full text of the order of the President of Republika Srpska down to Zvornik. And if we look at page 2, we see that on the basis of the above order by President Karadzic, Deputy Minister Kovac has issued the following order: Establish a public security station in Srebrenica on 12 July, appoint commanding officers, et cetera, take all necessary steps to ensure the protection of vital and other business facilities and property in general, the safety of citizens, and prevent the commission of crimes and breaches of law and order. And while implementing these measures ensure close co-operation with civil commissioner Miroslav Deronjic. Send daily reports on the progress of implementing the above measures to the office of the minister referring to the dispatch number as stated above. So if you can, if you have an opinion on this document, what is the significance of this order and the transmission of the president's order this way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, at its base value, it's an accurate reflection of how the order chain works, at least on the Ministry of the Interior side. When you read into the document, it reflects that the individuals have received by some means an awareness of what is happening in the town of Srebrenica and what steps need to be taken there in order to assert or reassert appropriate civilian control of the town. So in this case, I mean they're aware of what needs to happen. They're sending out various orders. They're reflecting that they know who needs to be co-operated with. In this case it's Mr. Deronjic. And again a verbatim listing of what orders are to be accomplished. And the fifth one that closes the loop on the orders and reporting chain is paragraph 5, where there is the expectation or order, if you were, just -- that daily reports on the progress of implementing these measures are to be sent to the office of the minister. So it's not a question of an order being given and no thought whatsoever as to whether or not compliance is -- is voluntary or whatever. He's making it clear that, you know, I want daily reports on this to ensure that -- that all aspects of the order are being complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we can see if we look at the first page of this document again that its number is 407/95. I'd like to now go -- this -- this exhibit has two exhibit numbers, Your Honour, the next one. It's P02996, and it's also P04373. So it's a duplicate, but either one of those, if I could have it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a document from chief of the CJB Zvornik, Dragomir Vasic. It's in tab 53, Mr. Butler. And we see at the top, Re: Dispatch number and it includes 40795. Acting -- in paragraph 1: "Acting in accordance with your dispatch I contacted the civilian commissioner in Bratunac, Miroslav Deronjic. "2. A meeting with General Mladic and General Krstic was held at the Bratunac Brigade command at 0800 hours," this is still 12 July, "at which tasks were assigned to all the participants. "3. The military operation is continuing according to plan. The Turks are fleeing towards Suceska while the civilians have gathered in Potocari, about 15.000." And then it goes on to talk about the establishment of the police station in Srebrenica, and in paragraph 5: "A meeting will be held at 10.00 with representatives of UNPROFOR and the International Red Cross and a Muslim representative from Srebrenica at which an agreement will be reached on the evacuation of the civilian population from Potocari to Kladanj." It's got in parentheses: "For them to have more problems there." It talks about trailer trucks for transport. And then 6: "Joint police forces," which we've seen in earlier documents, "are advancing on Potocari with the aim of taking UNPROFOR personnel prisoner, surrounding the entire civilian population and clearing the terrain of enemy groups." "You will be promptly informed of further facts and developments," in number 8. So I'd like your comment on this document keeping in mind the one we just saw from Tomo Kovac with the same number.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The previous document was the order with instructions to report back on compliance. This particular document is the first from Dragomir Vasic which essentially acknowledges, "I have received the order, and I am carrying out -- or beginning the process of carrying out the instructions that I've received." More than even that, Mr. Vasic is also providing additional information back to the benefit of the police forces staff in the office the minister as to what is happening in and around the Srebrenica area with respect to meetings with the military personnel, General Mladic and General Krstic, about tasks being assigned to participants, the military situation as Mr. Vasic understands it at the time, meetings that are upcoming with UNPROFOR and other representatives, and even noting that trailer trucks -- or in this case over a hundred trailer trucks have been provided for transport already. So even above noting that he has received and is complying with the orders, he's providing additional information to ensure that his superiors have full situational awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just -- we've heard a lot of evidence on it. I'm not going to try to go through all the events in Potocari on the 12th with you, but just remind us, what's the situation, if you recall, on the ground in Potocari early morning on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: At this point in time, the VRS and the police units have not yet moved into Potocari. They don't do that until after the third meeting which takes place beginning at 10.00 at the Hotel Fontana. So at this place in -- what you have in Potocari right now are the number of civilians from Srebrenica who have fled to Potocari, and they are still under the positive control of the Dutch UNPROFOR battalion forces that are in Potocari. So that is the situation as it exists in Potocari when this dispatch is being sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could now have 65 ter 3990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at tab 55, Mr. Butler. Another dispatch from chief of CJB. It's -- it says "illegible," but that would be Vasic. This is 12 July 1995. Very urgent. In the original we can see that handwritten at the top it says "Vasic." On the right. It's to police headquarters in Bijeljina and the office of the minister in Pale. And begins stating that at 1030 hours, a meeting was held at a hotel in Bratunac attended by the following: General Mladic, chief of centre Vasic, Miroslav Deronjic, president of the Municipal Assembly and Executive Council in Bratunac, Colonel Karremans, and I won't read through all the names of the people there, and then goes through a set of conclusions. According to Muslims there are 25.000 people in the base at Potocari, mainly small children, women and the elderly, and only 10 per cent are conscripts from 17 to 60 years old. They want to leave the camp voluntarily and go to Tuzla or Kladanj and they request assistance. They also request the free passage for able-bodied men because allegedly they are unarmed and they are not in contact with their army in the woods. Number 4: "After inspection depending on Mladic's decision, able-bodied men may be allowed to go in order to have others in the woods to surrender since our command urge them to do so." Five: "Acting upon President Karadzic's order which was conveyed to us today over the phone, the 2nd Company of the Zvornik PJP, two platoons, 60 men, shall be dispatched to Srebrenica with the task to secure all facilities of vital importance in the town and protect them from looting and misappropriation. They will carry out the task without co-operation of the military police which is busy with other tasks. "A platoon of this company will lie in ambush at Ravni Buljim, since Muslim groups were been spotted fleeing along this axis. You will be informed of further developments and facts." Can you comment on this document now after the last Hotel Fontana meeting on the 12th and what it says about the communications and command within the MUP chain?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: With respect to the information that Mr. Vasic is providing, I mean he's making a concerted and diligent effort to ensure that his superiors are informed of all of the developments that occurred relative to that third meeting, informing them of what General Mladic and the military have decided, what they have heard from the Muslims as to the number of civilians in Potocari and out of that number of civilians what the Muslims believe to be the percentage of military-aged men. It talks about the fact that General Mladic has made a decision regarding potentially screening the able-bodied men and that he may allow them to go as part of an effort to get other people to surrender. Paragraph 5 is particularly noteworthy insomuch as the fact that, you know, it notes a -- that Mr. Vasic received a telephonic order over the phone to dispatch elements of another PJP company to Srebrenica, and it was noted again -- whether it was President Karadzic personally calling or whether or not the person who called told Vasic that the order comes from President Karadzic is not quite clear, but certainly Mr. Vasic took it as an order from a proper authority and is letting his superiors in the chain of command, MUP chain of command, know that he is complying with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender this, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4935, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now D0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I now have D02023.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is at tab 56, Mr. Butler. This is a 12 July, 1240 hours intercept. And I'll just bring it up and then we'll go to another intercept from the same day. This is at -- we can see frequency 785.000, channel 5. It's headed: Inaudible, Panorama X-Y. Just again remind us what Panorama is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Panorama is the telephonic code-name for the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it says: [As read] "This morning," at the bottom, "we organised it here. We'll give them everything I talked with them and we will accept all of the civilians who want to and they can stay. Those who don't want to can choose where they'll go."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if I could have P04254. That might be MFI'd. This is another frequency, same channel, ten minutes later, between General Mladic and an unidentified male person. I'll just read it quickly. X says: "Go ahead, General." Mladic says: "Have these buses and trucks left?" X: "They have." Mladic: "When?" X: "Ten minutes ago." Mladic: "Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They've all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all - those who want to and those who don't want to." X: "I understand, General." And then there's some more conversation which I won't read out. What I want to ask you is: Militarily, what is the situation now at 12.50 on the 12th of July facing the VRS in Potocari in terms of threats or presence of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In that -- yes, in Potocari where the civilians are gathered?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Militarily there isn't any. At this juncture and time, the police and military forces that came down the road over the Yellow Bridge and into Potocari from the Bratunac area have entered the compound. Buses and trucks have entered the compound. They are already dealing with sorting individuals and putting the first people on buses. I believe the first bus convoy leaves Potocari somewhere around between 12.00 and 1230 hours on the 12th of July. And it's eminently clear to everyone that's there that there are no organised military forces of the ABiH at Potocari. It is completely demilitarised in the sense that not only is it mostly women, children, and elderly, those military-aged men who were there, they're not armed, and there's no indication overtly that they're even members of the armed forces. So they would have had that awareness very early on once the VRS and police forces entered Potocari on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, slightly wider than Potocari, what is the military situation for the VRS in the former enclave this time around 1.00 p.m. on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: By about 1300 on the 12th, the VRS which had been getting persistent reports of small enemy groups forming in columns near Jaglici and Susnjari and working their way out of the enclave and attempting to cross the road at Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje, there are now becoming enough of those reports that there's a -- a serious recognition on the part of the army that the forces of the ABiH aren't where they thought they were. The army's position going into the morning of 12 July 1995 was that since they did not encounter the bulk of the 28th Infantry Division in Srebrenica and there was no evidence that it was actually in Potocari, their view was that it had fallen further into the heart of the enclave area in an area referred to as the Bandera Triangle, which the United Nations had been prohibited by the Muslims from ever inspecting, and presumably preparing to break out towards the direction of Zepa from there. So most of the mobile military forces, the elements of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, the Birac Infantry Brigade, the Romanija Infantry Brigade, and the units that had actually -- you know, the Drina Wolves, the units that had actually captured Srebrenica were now moving to the west in order to engage the remaining forces of the 28th Infantry Division in the Bandera Triangle. By 1300, everyone's recognising that there's no contact being made with those forces. So by this point in time, everybody within the leadership structure of the military and the police there are recognising that the army isn't in fact in the Bandera Triangle. The ABiH forces are forming this column and attempting to go out over the road between Nova Kasaba-Konjevic Polje, and they also recognise that there are almost no forces there to interdict them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said earlier in the previous answer that the -- Potocari had effectively been demilitarised at this time, which was one of the goals of the leadership for the enclave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, correct in that sense, but I mean, the way that I look at it, there weren't armed elements of the 28th Infantry Division that accompanied any of the civilians from Srebrenica to Potocari. There were not armed soldiers there. There was no military presence there other than UNPROFOR. And as there has been, I presume, testimony and certainly evidence in other cases that I'm aware of, shortly after the VRS started arriving in Potocari, they begin disarming the Dutch Battalion soldiers. So very quickly, by the time the VRS and police forces arrived in Potocari on the 12th, there was absolutely no threat against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then at that time, the time of this intercept we see with General Mladic saying, "They've capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all - those who want to go and those who don't want to," from your analysis is there any military -- military justification for removing the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The -- in an abstract, clearly military commanders would want to remove or safeguard civilians from an area that they understood would be a potential battle-field where they can. While -- when one looks at -- there's the initial bit of confusion in the early morning hours of the 12th of July as to where the ABiH 28th Infantry Division is, whether it's in the Bandera Triangle or whether it's in the, you know, the column escaping out, there's no one from the VRS leadership, either in the Bratunac Brigade, the Drina Corps, the police staff, or the Main Staff, who's -- who's thinking that the ABiH 28th Infantry Division will somehow turn around and seek to attack Potocari. So there's no military threat in that context that would necessitate removing the population out of Potocari on that day under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move on to another document from about this time, 12 July, this is P04388. It's at tab 58, Mr. Butler, in your binder. This is a document signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic. It's a few hours later, actually, dated 12 July 1995, and it says 1730 hours on it. It's also got handwritten "Security administration chief of operation and training." It's to the Main Staff of the VRS, sector for intelligence and security and the command of the Drina Corps security. And it's been -- just remind us, who's Colonel Popovic in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Colonel Popovic is the chief of security for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He reports in paragraph 1: "In the course of the day our forces and MUP forces did not have any heavy exchange of fire with the Balijas. MUP forces entered Potocari in the morning without combat." And on the next page, paragraph 3: [As read] "A refugee group of about 30- to 35.000 women, children, and elderly, the infirm, and the sick is located after, beyond the UNPROFOR base towards Srebrenica, on the road and inside the facilities of the former factories. The security was established and the evacuation to Kladanj started. About 5.000 women and children were evacuated so far. We are separating men from 17 to 60 years of age and we are not transporting them. We have about 70 of them so far and the security organs and the DB," state security, "are working with them." So I wanted to ask you what you see as the significance of this very urgent report but also, from the military's perspective, what you would have to say about the fact that VRS security and state security are working with the prisoners, whatever that means exactly at the time.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, answering that particular question first, from a security perspective, either the military security organs or the state security organs, there would be legitimate purposes for wanting to question those captured men between the age of 17 and 60, presuming that some, if not all, had at least some knowledge of the military structure and situation as it existed in Srebrenica, who leadership figures might be, and what other valuable military or political information might be obtained from these individuals. So in that context, the fact that both the state security organs and the military security organs are working with them, and I take this working to be they are interrogating them to obtain this type of information, is what you might expect those organs to be doing. On the -- you know, there's another level because particularly within the context of state security organs and the security organs, there's also a law enforcement component. There are -- there was at least one list floating around and another list as well on individuals who are wanted potentially for their involvements for war crimes against the Serbs. And so there would also be a legitimate purpose to want to be questioning these individuals as to who they are, what their identities are, to ensure or to vet if these individuals are on those particular lists or, if not, do they know who these individuals are and where they might be located. So there would be -- there are normal legitimate purposes why these individuals will be interrogated by both the military and the MUP security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I ask you -- can I ask you in relation to that, we see this here on the 12th of July with the male prisoners. In your view, would it be routine or out of the ordinary in the context of captured prisoners in general, not specific to the Srebrenica operation, for both state security and VRS security to have contact with the prisoners and -- and question them, interrogate them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That would not be out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd now like to go to 65 ter 1942.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's in the second binder, Mr. Butler, tab 104. So it's far away. Now, this is from the head of the RDB, Dragan Kijac, 12 July 1995, to the deputy minister of the interior personally, Tomo Kovac, head of public security, and chief of RDB Bijeljina. Representatives -- I won't read out the whole thing but it's a report on the situation in Srebrenica and reports from international humanitarian organisations, and it states that -- what their information is that the morning on 12 July, the humanitarian situation was "worse than ever. The population lacks food, medicine and clothing." The estimates of 30.000 people around the DutchBat base, and it states that according to reports by military observers there's not a single armed soldier of the so-called BH Army among these people. Speaking about Potocari. The -- in the event of evacuation of the population via Zvornik as reportedly proposed by the Serbian side, the DutchBat commander propose that UNPROFOR provide 20 buses and complete the evacuation in rounds of about 1.000 people. So my question is: We saw state security working with the prisoners being present in Potocari in the last document. Can you comment on the information we see here being distributed up the MUP chain to various heads?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It reflects that state security is not exclusively talking to prisoners to gain information. They are also talking to members of the humanitarian organisation, and I take it from the context according to the reports by military observers, they're talking about the United Nations military observers who came up from Srebrenica and who were in Potocari and also sending reports back to the UN chain of command, that they're either accessing or they're talking to these individuals and gleaning information out of what they are reporting to their superiors. And in the context of that information, Mr. Kijac believes that it's important enough to ensure that the minister of the interior, the chief of the centre in Bijeljina and the head of the RJB, the public security department, they all personally see this report because it is of significance to what is developing, I would suspect primarily on the reports of the growing humanitarian crisis which would have an impact on the Republika Srpska from the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And based on your work in the Srebrenica investigation and your work on this case for the years that you were with the ICTY, the information regarding the humanitarian crisis that they're passing up, how accurate is it based on what you've seen from other documents, other sources?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
